title: From Perfect Spaces to Cantor–Bendixson
content: The module docstring frames the advance over the parent entry BairePerfectContinuum (OQ-01-OQ-02), which needs the WHOLE space to be perfect — a hypothesis that fails the moment the space has a single isolated point. The Cantor–Bendixson theorem removes it: every closed subset C of a second-countable space splits as C = V ∪ D with V countable and D perfect (exists_countable_union_perfect_of_isClosed). Mathlib's downstream corollary records only that D is nonempty, discarding the remainder V; this file keeps V and pushes two steps further — D is itself uncountable, and 𝔠 ≤ #D. Verified: no sorry, no axiom, no native_decide.
mathContext: Cantor–Bendixson: a closed set $C = V \cup D$ with $V$ countable, $D$ perfect; the perfect kernel of an uncountable $C$ is uncountable and of cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$.

title: The Perfect Kernel Is Uncountable — the New Content
content: exists_perfect_not_countable_subset is the heart of the entry and the open question's explicit request. From the decomposition C = V ∪ D (V countable, D perfect), if D were countable then C = V ∪ D would be countable (Countable.union), contradicting C uncountable — so ¬ D.Countable. This is a one-line topological argument that needs no metric or completeness, and its whole power lives in the remainder V that Mathlib's exists_perfect_nonempty_of_isClosed_of_not_countable throws away. exists_perfect_not_countable specialises it to the closed set univ (bridging ¬ Countable α to ¬(univ).Countable via countable_univ_iff), giving the whole-space form: every uncountable second-countable space contains a perfect, uncountable subset.
mathContext: $C = V \cup D$, $V$ countable, $C$ uncountable $\Rightarrow \neg\,D.\mathrm{Countable}$; the kernel inherits the uncountability of $C$.
prerequisites: countability of a union of countable sets

title: Cardinal Arithmetic and the Cantor-Scheme Bound
content: mk_nat_arrow_bool computes #(ℕ → Bool) = 2^ℵ₀ = 𝔠 (mk_arrow, mk_bool, mk_nat, two_power_aleph0). continuum_le_mk_of_perfect reproves the parent's bound inline so the file is self-contained: a nonempty perfect set in a complete metric space admits a continuous injection (ℕ → Bool) ↪ C (Perfect.exists_nat_bool_injection — the Cantor scheme embedding a copy of Cantor space). Corestricting that injection to the subtype C keeps it injective (Subtype.ext_iff), so 𝔠 = #(ℕ → Bool) ≤ #C by mk_le_of_injective. Completeness is exactly what the Cantor scheme needs to turn the perfect kernel into 2^ℵ₀ actual limit points.
mathContext: A nonempty perfect set in a complete metric space contains a homeomorphic copy of $2^{\mathbb N}$, so $\mathfrak{c} = \#(\mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Bool}) \le \#C$.
prerequisites: corestriction of an injection to a subtype

title: Cardinal Form and the Whole-Space Bound
content: exists_perfect_continuum_le_mk assembles the two halves: from exists_perfect_not_countable take the perfect uncountable kernel D, note an uncountable set is nonempty (an empty set is countable, contradicting ¬ D.Countable), then feed the nonempty perfect D into continuum_le_mk_of_perfect to get 𝔠 ≤ #D. The hypotheses MetricSpace + CompleteSpace + SecondCountableTopology are precisely 'uncountable Polish space'. continuum_le_mk then concludes 𝔠 ≤ #α because D injects into α (mk_set_le : #D ≤ #α, transitivity). This realises the open question's 'subset of cardinality 𝔠'.

title: Motivating Instance: ℝ Needs No Perfect-Space Hypothesis
content: exists_perfect_continuum_le_mk_real applies the cardinal form to ℝ, uncountable by not_countable_real (lifted from set to type via countable_univ_iff). ℝ happens to be perfect itself, but the theorem used no such hypothesis — the whole point is that the conclusion applies verbatim to uncountable Polish spaces WITH isolated points, exactly the case the parent's PerfectSpace bound cannot reach. With the matching upper bound #α ≤ 𝔠 for second-countable spaces, the kernel has #D = 𝔠 exactly, giving the perfect-set property: closed (indeed analytic) subsets of Polish spaces are countable or of size continuum, never strictly between — a theorem-level Continuum Hypothesis for closed sets.
mathContext: $\mathbb{R}$ contains a perfect, uncountable subset of cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$, obtained with no appeal to $\mathbb{R}$ being perfect.
prerequisites: the cardinal form of the theorem
